scope: Same complete 81-path review scope, all 112 obligations and ten shared scopes.

semantic_notes: The tied-run counterexample explicitly has equal returned lists, equal output lengths and permutation while both comparison and entry counts differ; returned value alone does not determine work.

Unsorted merge examples preserve both input lists as sublists for every Boolean comparator and therefore cannot repair their old inversion. The concrete measured result and size bounds hold without a sorted-input assumption.
Measured source/key value bridges require only decidable LE. Sortedness equivalence uses a linear preorder; the separate StableSort contract retains both sorted-input premises and key equality.
Signed record examples connect exact values and(2,3) counts. Generic arbitrary tagged payloads show left/right tie order and asymmetric(2,3)/(1,2) counts, with no payload equality typeclass.
The always-false comparator is input-locally key compatible for the all-equal-key record example and yields[C,A,B] with(1,2), setting up the explicit distinction between sortedness and stability.
The compatible always-false comparator yields a KeySorted permutation but explicitly not Stable, so compatibility is not silently used as a tie-stability premise.

The unsorted record merge gives[2C,1D,3A,1B] at(2,3), with equal-key filtered output[D,B] versus original[B,D] and explicit instability. This retains the necessity of sorted inputs for the standard key-merge stability contract.

TwoStage feeds the first returned merge into the second with zs as its left argument. Its value is merge zs(merge xs ys), entries equal comparisons+2, and its law-free size bounds are comparisons<=2*(|xs|+|ys|)+|zs| and entries<=that+2.
The comparison/entry projections use the corresponding actual AddMonoidHom and preserve the same measured bind and dependent first result. No independent cost recurrence replaces the computation.

The actual first/second stages have counts(1,2)/(2,3), composing to sorted[0,1,2] at(3,5). Deliberately substituting the original unsorted[2,0] instead of the returned first result gives[1,2,0] at(2,4), preserving the dependency counterexample.
